Intermittent air mixing system for anaerobic digestion of animal 
wastewater: Operating conditions and full-scale validation 
Hongnan Yang a,b, Liangwei Deng a,b,*, Jianwang Wu c, Wenguo Wang a,b, Dan Zheng a,b, 
Zhiyong Wang a,b, Yi Liu a,b 
a Biogas Institute of Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, Chengdu 610041, PR China 
b Key Laboratory of Development and Application of Rural Renewable Energy, Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, Chengdu 610041, PR China 
c Shijiazhuang Chengding Environmental Protection Technology Co. Ltd., Shijiazhuang 050000, PR China   
H I G H L I G H T S  
• Operating condition of air mixing for anaerobic digestion was investigated. 
• The maximum air mixing time was determined. 
• A full-scale digester was selected to investigate the feasibility of air mixing. 
• The air mixing was applied in full-scale plant successfully.  
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Air mixing 
Anaerobic digestion 
Effective methane production time 
Mixing time 
Swine wastewater 
A B S T R A C T   
An air mixing system for anaerobic digestion has been proved to be beneficial for methane production. The aim 
of the present study was to further investigate the appropriate conditions for air mixing. The effective methane 
production time (EMPT) was defined to determine the air mixing time in the article. The results indicated that 
the appropriate aeration intensity was 66.7 mL air per volume of reactor per min and mixing time was 1.5 min. 
When air mixing time exceeded 3 min on each occasion, total CH4 production was less than that achieved under 
the no mixing condition due to a decrease in the EMPT. In addition, the possibility of air mixing was evaluated in 
an anaerobic full-scale plant comprising a continuous stirred tank reactor. One year of operating data validated 
the feasibility of air mixing during the anaerobic digestion of swine wastewater.   
1. Introduction 
In China, large-scale and intensive livestock production results in the 
rapid increase of wastewater quantities in a few concentrated areas 
(Duan et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020b). According to the statistical data 
from National Bureau of Statistics of China (NBSC) (2017), annual ani­
mal wastewater production in China is about 3.8 billion tons, inclusive 
of both slaughtered and breeding stocks. The improper manure man­
agement has contributed to significant environmental problems (Pan­
telopoulos and Aronsson, 2021; Zhuang et al., 2020). It is estimated that 
livestock manure is responsible for 11%, 29%, and 52% of greenhouse 
gas (GHG) (such as CH4 and N2O), and NH3 emissions in China, 
respectively (Zhuang et al., 2019, 2020). Anaerobic digestion (AD) is the 
preferred method for animal wastewater treatment because of its 
beneficial effects in terms of waste disposal, renewable energy recovery, 
and greenhouse gas emission reduction (Deng et al., 2016; Tseng et al., 
2019). However, the AD of animal wastewater is limited by the low 
efficiency of biogas production and unstable operation because of low 
temperatures and slow degradation kinetics of complex organics in an­
imal wastewater (Deng et al., 2016). 
Mixing plays a prominent role in determining the efficiency of the 
anaerobic digestion process of animal wastewater. Appropriate mixing 
could improve the substrate-sludge contact with slight mass transfer 
resistance, enhance the hydrolysis step, ensure homogeneous distribu­
tion of substrate and micro-organisms and avoid settlings, scum and 
floating layers (Lindmark et al., 2014; Kariyama et al., 2018; Singh et al., 
2019; Wang et al., 2019). The three different types of mixing modes 
applied in AD comprise mechanical mixing, hydraulic mixing, and

biogas mixing (Kariyama et al., 2018). Many studies have investigated 
the impacts of different mixing modes on the biogas production effi­
ciency (Karim et al., 2005; Kariyama et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2019). 
Mechanical mixing can greatly enhance the disintegration of foam 
(scum) because of its large action radius. However, the high power 
dissipation under impeller mixing is expensive compared with biogas 
recirculation in terms of the maintenance/operating costs (Wu, 2012; 
Latha et al., 2019). For example, Trad et al. (2016) compared the energy 
consumption rates under mechanical mixing, hydraulic mixing, and 
biogas mixing, where the results showed that under the same shear level, 
the energy consumption was lower under biogas mixing than hydraulic 
mixing and mechanical mixing. Hydraulic mixing is usually only suit­
able for small reactors with low solid concentrations considering the 
occurrence of short circuits and dead zones (Karim et al., 2005; Bhat­
tacharjee et al., 2015). Biogas mixing is considered a simple and rapid 
alternative mixing technique for use in future AD plants because the 
absence of moving elements inside digesters reduces the amount of wear 
and maintenance (Dapelo et al., 2015; Kuczman et al., 2017). However, 
biogas mixing is not used frequently in on-farm biogas plants because it 
is difficult to maintain adequate mixing when the biogas production rate 
is low. 
Based on previous assessments of the impacts of micro-aeration on 
AD treatment (Lim and Wang, 2013; Lim et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2014; 
Peces et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2020a), a new mixing method for AD was 
developed in our previous research by using air as a gas source for 
mixing (referred to as “air mixing”) in order to solve the problems of 
insufficient biogas production and safety associated with biogas mixing 
(Yang and Deng, 2020). The feasibility of air mixing was demonstrated 
based on comparisons with other mixing modes (biogas mixing, me­
chanical mixing, and no mixing) at the same power input. The results 
indicated that air mixing had no negative effects on AD under limited 
aeration condition, and it could also improve the methane production 
efficiency and reduce the hydrogen sulfide (H2S) content of the biogas 
by 69% compared with reactors without air mixing (Yang and Deng, 
2020). However, the operating conditions for air mixing remain unclear 
and needs to be developed. Optimizing air mixing is essential for 
achieving effective mixing and improving the biogas quality, particu­
larly in terms of conditions such as the aeration intensity (or air flow 
rate), total volume of air for mixing, and mixing time. The aeration in­
tensity determines whether the substrate and sludge are mixed 
completely or effectively. The optimum volume of air avoids the nega­
tive effects of an excessive air volume, including the dilution of the 
methane content and the aerobic degradation of organic matter. An 
excessive air flow rate and mixing time will disrupt the reducing envi­
ronment for AD, and decrease the growth and activity of obligate an­
aerobes, especially methanogens, thereby negatively affecting the AD 
process. In addition, it is considered that air mixing is feasible for small- 
scale test equipment, but it is doubtful whether air mixing can be applied 
to full-scale anaerobic digesters. 
In the present study, in order to address the problems described 
above, the optimum conditions for air mixing were determined in order 
to develop the air mixing technique. The possibility of applying air 
mixing on an industrial scale was evaluated in a continuous biogas 
digester with a volume of 2000 m3. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Anaerobic digesters and materials 
A 4.5 L laboratory-scale air mixing reactor was established (Sup­
porting Information). The reactor had a working volume of 4.0 L and 
was mixed by introducing air into the reactor via a digital peristaltic 
pump and an aeration disc at the bottom of the reactor. The temperature 
was maintained at 35 ± 1◦C using a water jacket and thermostat. 
Swine wastewater is a typical type of animal wastewater. In this 
study, swine wastewater was used as the influent for a laboratory-scale 
experiment. The wastewater was collected from a swine farm located in 
Jianyang City, Sichuan Province, China. In order to avoid clogging 
problems in the reactor systems, large particles were sieved using a 6 
mesh screen (3.35 mm) after transporting the waste to the laboratory. 
The sieved swine wastewater was stored at 4◦C until use. The sludge 
inoculant for the AD experiments was harvested from a laboratory-scale 
mesophilic anaerobic digester used to treat swine wastewater (Sup­
porting Information). 
2.2. Experimental design 
2.2.1. Influence of aeration intensity on biogas production 
At the start of the experiment, 2 L of inoculum sludge was added to 
air mixed reactor. The reactor was fed swine wastewater once per day 
(semi-continuous mode) at a loading rate of 6.0 g VS/L/d. The steady 
state was defined as the point when biogas production varied within 
10% of the mean between the feeding times within 2–3 weeks. 
The aeration intensity was lowered from 66.7 mL/L/min to 33.3 mL/ 
L/min. The mixing times were 1.5, 3, 5, and 10 min. The biogas pro­
duction rate and biogas composition, as well as ORP were measured. The 
experiments were repeated in triplicate. 
2.2.2. Influence of different mixing conditions on mass transfer 
The mass transfer in a reactor was reflected by the distribution of the 
total solids (TS) within the reactor, which was determined by collecting 
samples for TS analysis from three different heights (10, 20, and 30 cm) 
above the base of the reactor after mixing. The coefficient of variance (κ) 
was defined as the ratio of the standard deviation in the TS concentra­
tions relative to the average TS concentration, as described by Eq. (1), 
and it was used to measure the degree of mixing. Furthermore, the 
“homogeneous mixing time” was defined as the time required to achieve 
a certain degree of mixing. In this study, a κ-value (less than 0.02) was 
considered to indicate homogeneous mixing.

2.2.3. Influence of mixing time on biogas production 
The air mixed reactor was operated as described in Section 2.2.1. The 
mixing times were set as 0, 1, 1.5, 3, 5, 10, 60, and 120 min. A constant 
aeration intensity of 66.7 mL/L/min was set for different mixing times 
and the mixing frequency was once per day. The biogas production rate 
and biogas composition were measured online at intervals of 10 min 
after feeding. ORP was monitored each day by an on-line probe. The 
experiments were repeated in triplicate. 
2.3. Full-scale validation 
Air mixing was performed for full-scale AD in a biogas plant that 
treated 150–300 m3/d of wastewater from swine farms with 
7000–16,000 pigs. The biogas plant also separated the low content 
liquid and concentrated liquid (Deng et al., 2014, 2016; Yang et al., 
2015; Liu et al., 2018). The raw swine wastewater was collected from a 
pig farm in a tank each day and then pumped into a sedimentation tank 
(see Supporting Information). Swine wastewater was separated into the 
concentrated liquid (50–100 m3/d) and low content liquid (100–200 
m3/d) by gravity sedimentation. The low content liquid and concen­
trated liquid were anaerobically treated by an upflow anaerobic sludge 
blanket (UASB) and continuous stirred tank reactor (CSTR), respec­
tively. The biogas was stored in a gasholder and used for power gener­
ation or to heat the piggery. The CSTR was mixed by air and heated by 
the excess heat from the biogas generator, whereas the UASB was not

mixed or heated. The digestion temperature in the CSTR was maintained 
at approximately 30◦C. The working volume of the full-scale CSTR 
reactor was 2000 m3, with a diameter of 16 m and height of 10 m. The 
biogas was stored in a double membrane gasholder with a working 
volume of 500 m3. The daily input quantity of the concentrated liquid in 
the CSTR was 53–106 m3 and the feed concentration was about 5% TS. 
The hydraulic retention time was 19–38 d. The organic loading rate of 
the reactor was 1.32–2.64 kg TS/m3/d. Air was compressed automati­
cally by an air compressor into a buffer tank with a volume of 1.0 m3 and 
pressure of 0.8 MPa (Supporting Information). To mix the reactor, 
compressed air was released into the reactor by opening the solenoid 
valve in the connecting pipe between the buffer tank and the air 
distributor in the reactor. The mixing frequency and mixing time were 
2–3 times per day and 1.5–2 min each time, respectively. The biogas 
plants were monitored for 12 months, where the biogas production and 
temperature were recorded each day. 
2.4. Analytical methods 
The Analyse of TS was performed according to standard methods 
(APHA, 1998). The ORP was monitored online by an ORP probe (InPro 
325X probe, M300 controller, Mettler Toledo, Urdof, Switzerland). The 
biogas produced in the bioreactors was collected in gas-tight bags. 
Biogas composition was determined using a gas chromatograph (GC) 
(SP-2100, Beijing Beifen-Ruili Analytical Instrument Co., Ltd., China) 
equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and a packed 
Porapak Q column (3 m × 3 mm). Helium gas was used as the carrier gas 
(flow rate 10 mL/min). The temperatures of the inlet, the oven and the 
TCD were 100, 100 and 55◦C, respectively. Details of the analytical 
methods were described in (Yang and Deng, 2020). 
2.5. Data analyses 
The SGompertz model equation was used to fit the CH4 concentration 
data curves and to determine the variation in the CH4 content over time. 
The formulas are showed in Eq. (2).

3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Optimized conditions for air mixing in AD 
The feasibility of air mixing in AD has been proved in our previous 
pilot study by compared the performance of AD reactors with different 
mixing modes (air mixing, biogas mixing, and no mixing) (Yang and 
Deng, 2020). The optimal conditions determined for air mixing in the 
AD process, such as the aeration intensity and time of air mixing, were 
presented in the following. 
3.1.1. Aeration intensity 
The power consumption required for mixing is likely to influence the 
economic cost of the process. The power input is generally 5–10 W/m3 
for biogas mixing (Metcalf et al., 2003) and was altered in each exper­
iment by varying the aeration intensity. When the aeration intensity was 
66.7 mL/L/min, the corresponding mixing power input was estimated to 
be about 5 W/m3. In order to reduce the consumption of electrical en­
ergy, the aeration intensity was reduced from 66.7 mL/L/min to 33.3 
mL/L/min, which corresponded to a power input of 2.5 W/m3. The 
effects of the power input on the mixing degree were presented in Fig. 1. 
As shown in Fig. 1, the κ value was 0.138 with a low aeration intensity of 
33.3 mL/L/min and mixing time of 1.5 min, which was much higher 
(one order of magnitude) than that (0.017) with the high aeration in­
tensity (66.7 mL/L/min) and the same mixing time. Furthermore, the 
low aeration intensity resulted in the stagnation at the bottom of the 
reactor and near the walls, although the upper zone at the top of the 
reactor was well mixed due to bubbles rupturing, as shown in Fig. 1(B). 
Fig. 1. Changes in the coefficient of variance (κ) (A) and total solids (TS) 
concentrations over time at mixing intensities of 33.3 mL/L/d (B) and 66.7 mL/ 
L/d (C).

When the mixing time increased to 10 min, homogeneous mixing was 
achieved (the κ value was equal to 0.023), but the power consumption 
was greatly increased due to the long mixing time. With a mixing time of 
3 min and aeration intensity of 33.3 mL/L/min, the consumption of 
electrical energy was equivalent to that with the higher aeration in­
tensity (66.7 mL/L/min) and a mixing time of 1.5 min. However, the κ 
value was still lower than that with the high aeration intensity (66.7 mL/ 
L/min) and the biogas production was 7.4% lower than that with the 
high aeration intensity (see Supporting Information). In addition, the 
low aeration intensity yielded a smaller quantity of gas from the reactor 
and the CH4 content of the biogas was slightly lower than that with the 
high aeration intensity. These results demonstrate that the power input 
for air mixing should exceed 2.5 W/m3 because it was difficult to ach­
ieve homogeneous mixing under this power input even with a long 
mixing time. 
It is expected that the percentage of dead zones will decrease and the 
mixing degree will increase as the aeration intensity (energy input) in­
creases (Wu, 2010; McLeod et al., 2018). However, the results obtained 
in previous studies indicate that this effect is very weak (Kariyama et al., 
2018). For example, increasing the gas circulation rate from 65 to 197 
mL/L/min did not significantly reduce the dead zones inside a flat 
bottom digester according to Karim et al. (2004). In addition, excessive 
aeration intensity can damage microbial flocs near the exits where 
strong turbulent flows exist and increasing the mixing input is uneco­
nomical (Zhang et al., 2016). The rheological properties and density of 
the liquid mixed should also be carefully considered when determining 
the appropriate aeration intensity. 
3.1.2. Effect of different air mixing time on biogas production 
The study of aeration intensity indicated that when the aeration in­
tensity was 66.7 mL/L/min, the air mixing system could achieve a ho­
mogeneous mixing in a short time (far below 10 min) and accordingly 
low amount of air used to mixing. The air mixing time was further 
optimized at the aeration intensity of 66.7 mL/L/min in terms of biogas 
production rate, biogas composition and methane production. 
3.1.2.1. Effect on biogas production rate. To investigate the effect of the 
air mixing time on biogas production, the biogas production rates (mL/ 
min) were measured under different air mixing times after mixing was 
stopped, as shown in Fig. 2. The biogas production rate was higher than 
that under no mixing (mixing time = 0 min) when the air mixing time 
did not exceed 5 min and the positive impact continued for about 5–6 h. 
The maximum biogas production rate was about 14.0 mL/min with 
mixing times in the range of 1.5–3 min, which was 75.0% higher than 
that under 8.0 mL/min with no mixing. Our observations showed that 
increasing the air mixing time did not significantly improve the pro­
duction of biogas. When the continuous mixing time exceeded 30 min, 
the biogas production rate decreased compared with that under no 
mixing. Similar results were obtained in previous studies of the three 
common types of mixing mode, where the digester was mixed well under 
an intermittent mixing mode with a relatively short mixing time (Kress 
et al., 2018; Mao et al., 2019). However, these results may have different 
explanations. In particular, a long air mixing time may have led to in­
hibition of the AD system due to the presence of air. In addition, the 
readily degradable organic matter may have been aerobically oxidized 
in the mixing stage to leave a high proportion of refractory substances, 
thereby reducing the gas production rate (Nguyen et al., 2019). 
3.1.2.2. Effect on biogas composition. The variations in the CH4 content 
were determined at different air mixing times (1, 1.5, 3, 5, 10, 30, 60, 
and 120 min) to estimate the appropriate air mixing time (Fig. 3). The 
response of the reactor to the injection of air (an oxidant) was very rapid 
and the CH4 content dropped markedly from 58% to below 1% as the air 
mixing time increased from 0 to more than 15 min (Fig. 3(A)). Although 
the air mixing time was as long as 2 h, the CH4 content gradually 
returned to its threshold value when air mixing stopped as shown in 
Fig. 3(B) and the ORP value returned to less than −400 mV (see Sup­
porting Information), which indicated the AD systems were not dis­
rupted. Therefore, the air mixing time and subsequent recovery time for 
the CH4 content were key factors that determined the appropriate air 
mixing time. 
The variation in the CH4 content over time after air mixing stopped 
could be described by Eq. (2). The fitted results obtained for different air 
mixing times are shown in Table 1, where the R2 values over 0.9 indicate 
that the fitted results were good. The recovery time required for the CH4 
content to recover to a certain value was calculated using Eq. (2). The 
threshold value for the CH4 content was determined as 40%. The cor­
responding recovery times for different air mixing tines are shown in 
Table 2. The results demonstrate that the recovery time increased from 
0.08 h to 3.83 h as an increase of air mixing time and it took more than 1 
h to reach the threshold value of 40% when the air mixing time was 
more than 3 h. 
3.1.2.3. Optimum air mixing time. The results presented above demon­
strate that a long air mixing time had negative impacts on the biogas 
production rate and biogas composition, thereby affecting methane 
production. We then determined the maximum acceptable mixing time 
for which the methane production could not be lower than that with no 
mixing. Two new metrics were developed to compare the results. The 
first metric called the “non-effective CH4 production time (NEMPT)” was 
defined as the time when the CH4 content dropped below a specified 
threshold (40% in this study) after air mixing. The other metric was the 
converse of NEMPT, i.e., the “effective CH4 production time (EMPT),” 
which was defined as the difference between 24 h and NEMPT. The 
NEMPT, EMPT, CH4 production rate (PrCH4), and total CH4 production 
volume (PCH4) within EMPT under different mixing times are summa­
rized in Table 2. The total CH4 production (PCH4) was calculated as PrCH4 
multiplied by EMPT. As shown in Table 1, a long mixing time resulted in 
a shorter EMPT and the EMPT decreased greatly to only 18.17 h under 
continuous mixing for 2 h on each occasion. When the air mixing time 
was less than 3 min, PCH4 exceeded that under no mixing, and the largest 
PCH4 was obtained when the mixing time was 1.5 min. These results 
indicated that the maximum air mixing time should be 3 min at an 
aeration intensity of 66.7 mL/L/min, and the appropriate air mixing 
time was 1.5 min. A mixing time of 1.5 min produced the greatest 
amount of CH4 and minimized the consumption of electrical energy to 
make the process more economical.

3.2. Validation based on a full-scale anaerobic digester 
Air mixing was applied in a full-scale anaerobic digester for treating 
swine wastewater to validate further its feasibility. The aeration in­
tensity and mixing time were set as 3.0–4.5 mL/L/min and 1.5–2 min, 
respectively, in the full-scale anaerobic digester (see Section 2.3). The 
aeration intensity approached the limit of 5–7 mL/L/min recommended 
by Metcalf et al. (2003) for biogas mixing and its corresponding power 
input was 3.5–5 W/m3. These design parameters closed to optimum 
condition obtained from the laboratory scale experiment as described in 
Section 3.1 that the power input for air mixing should exceed 2.5 W/m3 
in view of degree of mixing and mixing performance, and the air mixing

time should not exceed 3 min when the aeration intensity was 66.7 mL/ 
L/min (the corresponding power input of 5 W/m3). The full-scale 
anaerobic digester with air mixing system has been running steadily 
for 5 years. Over the past 5 years, the inlet, outlet, and slag discharge 
were not blocked, whereas these problems affected other biogas projects 
for swine wastewater treatment, thereby demonstrating that air mixing 
was highly effective. 
The full-scale anaerobic digester was monitored for 1 year to inves­
tigate the long-term effect of air mixing on biogas production. The 
biogas production data obtained over 1 year are shown in Fig. 4. The 
volumetric biogas production rate per day varied among 0.252–0.457 
m3/m3/d and the mean value was 0.352 m3/m3/d. The biogas produced 
from April to September was used for power generation, and the power 
generation production per month was in the range of 10558–26069 kW/ 
h. In winter (January and October to December), the biogas was used for 
combustion and it normally heated the boiler. The results showed that 
air injection did not affect the quality of the biogas. In addition, the 
reactor normally produced biogas, which could be used to generate 
electricity and as boiler fuel. Air mixing had no negative effects on 
biogas production and the biogas quality in AD system. In addition, due 
to the separation of the low content liquid and concentrated liquid, the 
AD fermentation tank still maintained a digestion temperature of 30◦C 
when the temperature was below −10◦C in the winter. In contrast, if the 
traditional process (heating all raw waste water) was adopted for swine 
wastewater with TS 1.0–1.5%, it was not possible to raise the digestion 
temperature to 30◦C by using the waste heat from power generation. 
Thus, a biogas reactor for swine wastewater treatment could not operate 
normally in the winter without additional heating. Therefore, our 
operational performance assessment of the full-scale anaerobic reactor 
demonstrated that air mixing is feasible for application in the industry. 
4. Conclusion 
Operation condition in an air mixing system for anaerobic digestion 
was evaluated in lab-scale experiments. The appropriate aeration in­
tensity was 66.7 mL/L/min and mixing time was 1.5 min. The air mixing 
time should not exceed 3 min because long mixing time led to a decrease 
in the effective methane production time and accordingly total CH4 
production. Validation of air mixing based on a full-scale anaerobic 
digester was conducted at the aeration intensity of as 3.0–4.5 mL/L/min 
and the mixing time of 1.5–2 min. Stable operation and biogas pro­
duction over one year demonstrated the feasibility of air mixing.
